 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 Didn't imagine it: Pentagon admits U.S. was not prepared for drone warfare .

 Memory costs: Nintendo ( NTDOY ) Switch 2 unit sales tank after price hikes .

 Re-routing: Trump-Putin diesel deal at risk as U.S.-bound tankers change course .
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Pocketbook policy 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
 U.S. stocks rallied broadly on Wednesday after Democrats won control of Congress in a midterm election landslide. Markets tend to like the sense of certainty surrounding gridlock, as well as checks related to tariffs and affordability, government spending, or scrutiny on Big Tech that might limit their capex . While Washington captured the headlines, voters also weighed in on pivotal state-level economic initiatives that signaled where fiscal policy is heading nationwide.

 Florida Amendment 3: Homeowners are set to get a big break as the tax-free value on primary homes jumps from $50K to $150K next year (and $250K in 2028) for non-school property taxes. Landlords and local businesses benefit too because the maximum yearly increase on their taxable property value will be cut in half from 10% to 5%. However, new residents moving to the state will have to wait five years with the old $50K break before they can unlock the expanded relief. (Approved 62.0% to 38.0%)

 California Proposition 40: This measure would've slapped billionaire residents with a one-time 5% tax on their total worldwide wealth to fund state healthcare, public schools, and food assistance programs. It didn't pass, likely because of fears it would discourage California business investment or risk expanding to millionaires and the middle class. It may have also been seen as promoting "one-time" capital levies instead of structurally balanced budgets. (Rejected 55.3% to 44.7%)

 Arizona Proposition 316: With affordability on the ballot, this initiative targeted supermarket inflation by freezing new taxes and increases through June 30, 2027. After that, local governments need voter approval to introduce or raise grocery taxes, subject to a 2% ceiling, while existing rates at or above 2% can remain but cannot increase. It aims to protect household budgets for consumers while encouraging fiscal restraint across municipal governments. (Passed 61.5% to 38.5%)
